# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

1	# The task dashboard
2	
3	A read-only view of what a repo's Claudinite scheduler is doing — the declared task
4	roster, the live work-item queue, the outcome history, and the Actions runs behind
5	them — on one page. It is part of the engine, so every member gets it in its mount
6	at `.claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/dashboard/` and any of them can serve it.
7	
8	It has **two views**, and which one you land on is the URL:
9	
10	- **Fleet** — every member at once, worst first. What a deployment with a roster
11	  opens on.
12	- **Repo** — one member's scheduler in full. Reached by clicking a member, or
13	  `?repo=owner/name` directly.
14	
15	A deployment with one member (or none) goes straight to the repo view: a one-row
16	fleet overview would be nothing but a click in the way.
17	
18	## Running it
19	
20	Locally, against a checkout:
21	
22	```sh
23	node engine/scheduler/dashboard/serve.mjs missingbulb/Claudinite
24	```
25	
26	Deployed, it is static files behind any web server — including GitHub Pages. See
27	**Deploying** below for the one file a deployment adds.
28	
29	## What it shows
30	
31	| Panel | Answers |
32	|---|---|
33	| **Stat tiles** | How many tasks exist, what is open, what is parked or past a leash, what is running, when the next anchor falls |
34	| **Task roster** | Every *declared* task — cadence, model, outcome ceiling, precondition signals, its current work item, its next anchor, its outcome history |
35	| **Queue** | Open `[claudinite-work]` items by state, what each waits on, how long it has sat, and which recovery rule is about to claim it |
36	| **Scheduler runs** | Recent and in-flight Actions runs |
37	
38	A task with no work item still gets a row: "never ran" is usually the thing you
39	opened this for, and an issue-derived list would omit it silently.
40	
41	## The fleet view
42	
43	A fleet page answers a different question from the per-repo one. Per repo it is
44	"what is this scheduler doing"; across a fleet it is **"where do I need to look"** —
45	and a page that answers the first question twelve times over does not answer the
46	second. So nothing on it is a total for its own sake.
47	
48	| Panel | Answers |
49	|---|---|
50	| **Rollup tiles** | How many *members* need a human — not how many items exist |
51	| **Members** | Every member ranked worst-first: its health with reasons, its open queue mix, recent outcomes, scheduler health, mount freshness, task count |
52	| **Tasks across the fleet** | One task, everywhere it runs — a shared pack's task parked in four members at once is a canon problem no single repo's page reveals |
53	| **Pack adoption** | Which packs are in use and how widely — who a change to a pack would reach |
54	
55	Three rules shape it, and they are in [`fleet.mjs`](fleet.mjs):
56	
57	**Attention is earned, not counted.** A member surfaces because something is *true*
58	of it — an item parked, a leash blown, a scheduler failing, a mount that stopped
59	converging — and each arrives as a reason with a severity, never as a number to be
60	summed. One parked item outranks forty healthy work items.
61	
62	**Absence is a state.** A member that does not run Claudinite, one you cannot read,
63	and one that is running fine are three different answers and never collapse into
64	"0". Not being able to see a repo is a permissions fact reported quietly, not an
65	alarm competing with a genuinely broken member.
66	
67	**One member's failure is one row's problem.** Every member is summarised
68	independently, so a private repo or a rate-limit stumble becomes a row that says so
69	rather than a blank page.
70	
71	Two signals are visible *only* here, because no single repo's page has the
72	comparison:
73	
74	- **Mount drift** — each member's `ref` and `engineVersion` against the canon's.
75	  Judged on those and never on `updated` alone, since a held stamp pins `updated`
76	  behind a pending note while the mount converges normally. Needs `canonRepo` in the
77	  config; without it freshness reads *unknown* rather than being guessed.
78	- **A scheduler that never ran** — a member that declares tasks and has never
79	  produced a work item is not idle, it is unwired. Every per-repo number for it is a
80	  perfectly healthy zero.
81	
82	## Who it runs as
83	
84	**The viewer, and only the viewer.** There is no backend, no shared credential and
85	no service account: the page calls `api.github.com` from the browser as whoever is
86	using it, so it can show nobody anything their own GitHub account cannot already
87	read. The credential lives in `sessionStorage` and dies with the tab.
88	
89	Two ways to get one:
90	
91	- **Sign in with GitHub** — a button, no typing. Available when the deployment
92	  configures `clientId` and `exchangeUrl`.
93	- **A pasted token** — the fallback, and the local-development path. Needs
94	  read-only **Contents**, **Issues** and **Actions**.
95	
96	### Why "just use my existing GitHub login" is not on that list
97	
98	It cannot be. A browser will not send github.com's session cookies to
99	`api.github.com`, and the API does not accept cookie auth cross-origin at all —
100	"already logged in to GitHub" is not a credential a web page can spend. Every
101	GitHub-backed dashboard you have used either asked for a token or ran an OAuth
102	sign-in; there is no third option.
103	
104	Sign-in is the closest thing, and it is genuinely *your* permissions: after one
105	authorization, every call runs as you. The only piece that cannot live in the page
106	is the `code` → token exchange, which needs the app's client secret **and** hits an
107	endpoint that sends no CORS headers. That is what `exchangeUrl` points at —
108	[`oauth-exchange.example.mjs`](oauth-exchange.example.mjs) is a deployable
109	implementation. It sees one code, returns one token, and never touches repo data.
110	
111	## Caching
112	
113	A fleet view is only affordable because most of what it reads does not change.
114	Three strategies, because the data has three shapes — see
115	[`cache.mjs`](cache.mjs):
116	
117	| Data | Strategy | Why |
118	|---|---|---|
119	| Repo content (task declarations, the tree) | keyed by **commit SHA**, never expires | a path at a sha cannot change, so an unmoved `main` costs zero calls |
120	| Open items, runs, repo metadata | **ETag** revalidation | a `304` is free — it does not count against the rate limit, so this is fresh data at no cost |
121	| Closed-issue history pages | **24h TTL** | settled, but not addressable by a sha |
122	
123	Measured on this repo, cold versus warm: **21 requests → 4**, and the warm load
124	spends **zero** rate limit (its four requests are all 304s). The open queue is still
125	never stale — only settled history ages.
126

---
name: adopt-pack
description: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
---

Adding a pack to a repo that already runs Claudinite. Whole-repo bootstrap and the on-demand
refresh are [adopt-claudinite](../adopt-claudinite/SKILL.md); this is the narrower act of turning
one or more packs on. The declaration is authoritative — declaring is the project's call — so the
work is: declare, answer what the pack asks, materialize its content, satisfy what it now demands.

## 1. Declare

The full directory of adoptable packs — every canon pack with what it covers, how it activates,
and what it requires — is vendored in the mount at `.claudinite/shared/packs/directory.GENERATED.md`
(canon-side: `packs/directory.GENERATED.md`); read it when choosing, or when the owner asks what
could be added. **Match the owner's plain-words name to a pack id yourself** before asking them to
disambiguate — pack ids rarely read like how people describe them, so read the candidate's entry
there and confirm the fit.

Add each chosen pack's id to `packs` in `.claudinite-checks.json`. A pack that only makes sense
alongside another names it in `requires`; `resolveDeclaredPacks` pulls that closure in when the
declaration is written, so you declare what you *chose* and its dependencies follow (e.g.
`spec-driven-product` pulls `executable-requirements`). An unknown pack name — or an unknown
property on an entry — is a blocking **settings** error, not a conformance finding; fix the name.

## 2. Interview — the part that is easy to skip and must not be

A pack that needs the project's intent before it can provide value declares `questions` on its
manifest (see [packs/README.md](../../../README.md) and the machinery in
[../adopt-claudinite/interview.mjs](../adopt-claudinite/interview.mjs)). For **every** newly
declared pack that asks questions:

- Where a question says the repo may already hold the answer (a product brief, an existing
  requirements doc, the issue tracker), **read that first and confirm** rather than asking cold.
- Otherwise ask the owner directly (`AskUserQuestion`), one question at a time, at the point of
  adoption — when a human asked for the adoption, they are present by construction.
- Record each answer **verbatim** on that pack's entry as `answers: { "<question-id>": "<text>" }`.
  `"n/a — none wanted"` is a valid answer and stops the asking. Where the question carries a
  `distill` note, derive the entry's `config` from the answer (e.g. `executable-requirements`'s
  spec path → `config.spec`).

### When nobody is there to ask

Adoption also runs **unattended** — a scheduled task acting on a recommendation, the
fleet-add-missing-packs task's agent stage, any run with no human in the loop. The interview is then the hard stop, and
the order matters:

1. **Never guess an answer, and never leave the question unrecorded.** A pack whose question is
   answered by inference carries a decision nobody made, in a file that then propagates by
   `requires` closure and outlives whoever could have corrected it. `"n/a"` is an *owner's* answer,
   not a default you may write on their behalf.
2. **Finish everything the question does not gate, first** — declare, re-vendor, refresh the badge
   row, scaffold, and get the checks green (§4, §5). Stopping at the question with a red repo hands
   the owner a broken tree *and* a question; stopping with a green one hands them only the question.
3. **Then stop, and hand off in the open.** Open the PR with what is settled, name each unanswered
   question in the PR body under a heading that says the adoption is incomplete, and say the same
   on whatever issue prompted the run. Do **not** merge, do not proceed to a next pack's interview,
   and do not re-run the adoption on a later firing hoping the answer appeared — an unanswered
   question is a human's, and re-asking it weekly is nagging.

A pack that asks nothing adopts fully unattended; this section costs it nothing.

## 3. Re-vendor

The new packs' prose, checks, and skills must land under the tracked `.claudinite/shared/` mount,
**and the repo must be stamped with the version it is now at.** Fetch a fresh canon to scratch and
run its install runner against the checkout — sessions never fetch:

```
node <canon>/updates/install.mjs --target . <pack-id> [<pack-id>…]
```

**Do not hand-roll this with `apply-vendor-set.mjs`.** It lays the files down correctly and does one
thing that nothing notices for weeks: it stamps **every declared pack** at the newest version,
whether or not the records between were ever applied. `migrationApplies` is `want > have`, so once
the stamp reaches a record's own version that record stops applying — not for this cycle, but
permanently. Re-vendoring a repo to add one pack therefore silently burns every pending record for
the packs it *already* had, and the repo is left claiming a version whose shape it was never
migrated into.

content.content:
That is correct behaviour at version zero, where there is no older state to skip; it is wrong
everywhere else, and adding a pack to a live repo is everywhere else.

The runner declares each pack, vendors its content, stamps it and every pack in its `requires`
closure at the newest version, runs any one-shot seed ops, and gates on the converged tree's own
self-test. It exits non-zero on a refusal or an unanswered interview — a pack already installed is
**refused**, because reinstalling would restamp the repo to the newest version while skipping every
record in between.

Then **refresh the README pack-badge row**, from the mount you just rebuilt:

```
node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/converge-wiring.mjs <owner/repo> --badges
```

Declaring a pack is what makes that row wrong, and adoption is the only moment anything derives it —
the nightly deliberately leaves a repo's README alone, so a row not refreshed here stays stale until
someone notices by eye. The converge rewrites the row in place between its
`<!-- claudinite:packs -->` markers, keeping whatever the repo wrote after the closing one, and is a
no-op when the row is already right. A repo that has deleted its row keeps it deleted only if you
skip this — dropping the row is a real choice, so don't re-seed one the repo removed on purpose.

## 4. Scaffold what the pack now demands

A newly active pack may require structure the repo doesn't have yet — deliberately, so the
declaration is a statement of intent that its own findings then guide you to satisfy. Run the
world sweep and let each finding name the file: e.g. `product-wiki` wants its index and the
reviewed `product-requirements/` sink before the isolation wall has anything to guard. Scaffold
per the pack's own README template; the pack's rules are the checklist.

## 5. Land

World and work checks green (`.claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs`; the Stop hook
carries the work checks). Commit referencing the task's issue, push, open one PR. Content a pack
seeds through this flow — a `product-wiki` wiki's first researched, cited pages — rides the same
review gate as any other change; it is never pushed straight to the default branch.

**A failing check is your work, not the reviewer's.** Declaring a pack is what switched those rules
on, so every finding they now produce belongs to this change — fix it here, in the repo, before the
PR opens. Two things that are *not* fixes: silencing a rule by adding it to `rules`/`accept` in
`.claudinite-checks.json`, and undeclaring the pack to make the findings stop. Both turn a real
signal off on the repo's first exposure to it. If a finding genuinely cannot be satisfied — the pack
demands structure this repo has decided against — that is evidence the pack is **not** the right fit:
drop it from the declaration, say why on the PR, and let the smaller adoption land.

**Never leave the repo red.** Whatever stops you — a check you cannot satisfy, an unanswered
interview question, a scaffold that needs a decision — get the tree green first and open the PR on
what is settled. An incomplete adoption in a green repo is a handoff; an incomplete adoption in a
red one is a bug report against you.

# Publish the Claudinite task dashboard to GitHub Pages.
#
# SEEDED ONCE, AT ADOPTION, and this repo's from that moment. `.github/workflows/` is
# the one directory the nightly update cannot push to — the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` is
# refused there — so this file arrives with the adopting session and never converges.
# That is why it is a thin shim: everything that can be updated lives in the mount, and
# only what must be frozen is frozen here.
#
# The site holds NO repository data. It is a shell that calls the GitHub API from the
# viewer's own browser with the viewer's own credential, so publishing it discloses
# nothing a viewer could not already read — someone who cannot see a repo sees nothing
# of it here. Do not bake API responses into the build; that property is the reason a
# public Pages site is a safe host for it.
#
# Configure it in `.claudinite-checks.json`, on the `claudinite-dashboard` entry's
# `config` — not here. Every key is optional.

name: Claudinite dashboard

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths:
      # The mount is the page's source, so a converge that moves it republishes.
      - '.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-dashboard/**'
      - '.claudinite/shared/engine/**'
      - '.claudinite-checks.json'
      - '.github/workflows/claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml'
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

# Never two deployments at once, and a superseded build is not worth finishing.
concurrency:
  group: claudinite-dashboard-pages
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 24

      - name: Assemble the site
        run: node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-dashboard/build-site.mjs

      # The build exits clean with no `_site` when the mount does not yet carry the
      # dashboard — adopted, not yet converged. Uploading nothing would fail the run,
      # and deploying an empty artifact would replace a working site with a 404.
      - name: Is there a site to publish?
        id: built
        run: |
          if [ -f _site/index.html ]; then
            echo "ready=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "ready=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            echo "No _site/index.html — skipping the deploy until the mount carries the dashboard."
          fi

      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5
        if: steps.built.outputs.ready == 'true'

      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        if: steps.built.outputs.ready == 'true'
        with:
          path: _site

    outputs:
      ready: ${{ steps.built.outputs.ready }}

  deploy:
    needs: build
    if: needs.build.outputs.ready == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

+# Publish the Claudinite task dashboard to GitHub Pages.
+#
+# SEEDED ONCE, AT ADOPTION, and this repo's from that moment. `.github/workflows/` is
+# the one directory the nightly update cannot push to — the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` is
+# refused there — so this file arrives with the adopting session and never converges.
+# That is why it is a thin shim: everything that can be updated lives in the mount, and
+# only what must be frozen is frozen here.
+#
+# The site holds NO repository data. It is a shell that calls the GitHub API from the
+# viewer's own browser with the viewer's own credential, so publishing it discloses
+# nothing a viewer could not already read — someone who cannot see a repo sees nothing
+# of it here. Do not bake API responses into the build; that property is the reason a
+# public Pages site is a safe host for it.
+#
+# Configure it in `.claudinite-checks.json`, on the `claudinite-dashboard` entry's
+# `config` — not here. Every key is optional.
+
+name: Claudinite dashboard
+
+on:
+  push:
+    branches: [main]
+    paths:
+      # The mount is the page's source, so a converge that moves it republishes.
+      - '.claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-dashboard/**'
+      - '.claudinite/shared/engine/**'
+      - '.claudinite-checks.json'
+      - '.github/workflows/claudinite-dashboard-pages.yml'
+  workflow_dispatch:
+
+permissions:
+  contents: read
+  pages: write
+  id-token: write
+
+# Never two deployments at once, and a superseded build is not worth finishing.
+concurrency:
+  group: claudinite-dashboard-pages
+  cancel-in-progress: true
+
+jobs:
+  build:
+    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    steps:
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
+      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
+        with:
+          node-version: 24
+
+      - name: Assemble the site
+        run: node .claudinite/shared/packs/claudinite-dashboard/build-site.mjs
+
+      # The build exits clean with no `_site` when the mount does not yet carry the
+      # dashboard — adopted, not yet converged. Uploading nothing would fail the run,
+      # and deploying an empty artifact would replace a working site with a 404.
+      - name: Is there a site to publish?
+        id: built
+        run: |
+          if [ -f _site/index.html ]; then
+            echo "ready=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
+          else
+            echo "ready=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
+            echo "No _site/index.html — skipping the deploy until the mount carries the dashboard."
+          fi
+
+      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5
+        if: steps.built.outputs.ready == 'true'
+
+      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
+        if: steps.built.outputs.ready == 'true'
+        with:
+          path: _site
+
+    outputs:
+      ready: ${{ steps.built.outputs.ready }}
+
+  deploy:
+    needs: build
+    if: needs.build.outputs.ready == 'true'
+    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    environment:
+      name: github-pages
+      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
+    steps:
+      - id: deployment
+        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

+// claudinite-dashboard — a browser view of what a repo's (or a fleet's) Claudinite
+// scheduler is doing, published as a static site.
+//
+// WHY A PACK AND NOT ENGINE CODE. The dashboard is not part of running the scheduler:
+// nothing converges, ticks or executes because it exists, and a member that never
+// looks at it should not carry it. Engine code is what every member runs; this is
+// content a member OPTS INTO, and adoptable content in this corpus is a pack. That
+// also buys it the things a pack has and engine code does not — its own version and
+// migration lane, a declaration that gates it, and an adoption moment at which its
+// deployment can be wired.
+//
+// WHAT IT READS. Only the queue's own vocabulary and the task declarations at HEAD,
+// through the engine modules that define them (`../../engine/scheduler/queue/*`), so
+// the page cannot drift from the mechanism it renders. Those relative paths resolve
+// identically in the canon (`packs/<id>/` beside `engine/`) and in a member's mount
+// (`.claudinite/shared/packs/<id>/` beside `.claudinite/shared/engine/`), which is
+// why the pack can be read straight out of the mount with nothing rewritten.
+//
+// NO CHECKS, NO PROSE. It enforces nothing and there is no way to write the dashboard
+// wrongly in a consuming repo — it is a page, not a practice. Prose here would cost
+// every session in every declaring repo tokens for something no session acts on, so
+// its README carries the explanation instead and `prose` stays null.
+//
+// PUBLISHING IS THE ADOPTION MOMENT. `.github/workflows/` is the one directory the
+// nightly update can never push to (the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` is refused there), so
+// a deploy workflow can only arrive by being SEEDED — written by the install flow and
+// committed by the adopting session, which holds a credential the Action does not.
+// Hence the `seedOps` entry: adopting the pack is what wires the Pages deploy, and
+// the workflow is the member's from the moment it lands.
+//
+// THE BUILD SCRIPT DELIBERATELY IS NOT SEEDED. `build-site.mjs` lives in the pack and
+// is read out of the mount by the seeded workflow, exactly as the scheduler stub reads
+// the engine's tick. So the assembly logic keeps converging with the canon while the
+// workflow — the part that cannot converge — stays a one-time seed. Only the file that
+// has to be frozen is frozen.
+export default {
+  id: 'claudinite-dashboard',
+  version: 1,
+  minEngineVersion: 4,
+  ruleRoutingGuidance: {
+    belongs: 'the browser dashboard over Claudinite scheduler state, and the static site that publishes it',
+    excludes: 'how the scheduler behaves — core; workflow practice — github-actions; product sites — static-website',
+  },
+  badge: 'badge.svg',
+
+  // Never fingerprinted. Nothing in a repo's shape implies wanting a dashboard, and a
+  // scan that suspected one from the presence of a scheduler would suspect it in every
+  // member on the fleet.
+  detect: null,
+  marker: null,
+  seededByDefault: false,
+
+  // A page, not a practice — see the header.
+  prose: null,
+  worldRules: [],
+  workRules: [],
+
+  // Nothing to ask. Every fork this pack has is answered by a default that is right for
+  // nearly every project: a member's dashboard shows that member, signs in with a
+  // pasted token, and compares against no canon. The fleet deployment — one repo, not
+  // twelve — says so in its declaration's `config`, which is read as optional
+  // throughout: an unset key is the default, never a misconfiguration.
+  //
+  // config keys, all optional:
+  //   canonRepo   — the reference member mounts are compared against (fleet view)
+  //   rosterUrl   — a roster artifact; more than one member makes the fleet the landing view
+  //   repos       — an inline roster instead of a URL
+  //   clientId    — GitHub App / OAuth App client id, for the sign-in button
+  //   exchangeUrl — the code-to-token endpoint that sign-in needs
+  questions: [],
+
+  // Seeded, never converged: `.github/workflows/` cannot be written by the nightly, so
+  // this arrives once, at adoption, and the repo owns it from there. It is a thin shim
+  // over `build-site.mjs` in the mount for exactly that reason — the part that cannot
+  // be updated is kept as small as possible.

input.body:
Closes #934. Human-only setup: #942. Supersedes and closes missingbulb/Sheepdog#232.

A new opt-in pack, `packs/claudinite-dashboard/`, carrying a browser view of what a repo's — or a fleet's — Claudinite scheduler is doing, and publishing it to GitHub Pages.

## Adopting it

```jsonc
{ "packs": ["claudinite-dashboard"] }
```

That's the whole of it for a member: covers this repo, pasted-token sign-in, publishes to Pages. **Adoption wires the deploy** — `seedOps` writes the workflow into `.github/workflows/`. Optional `config` adds a roster (`rosterFile`/`repos`), a `canonRepo` for mount-drift, and `clientId`+`exchangeUrl` for Sign in with GitHub.

## Why a pack, not engine code

Nothing converges, ticks or executes because the dashboard exists, and a member that never looks at it shouldn't carry it. Engine code is what every member *runs*; this is content a member opts into — and being a pack buys a version and migration lane, a declaration that gates it, and an adoption moment to wire the deploy at.

## The one structural insight

**`.github/workflows/` is the one directory the nightly update can never push to** — the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` is refused there. So a deploy workflow can only arrive by being *seeded*: written by the install flow and committed by the adopting session, which holds a credential the Action doesn't. That's why adoption is the wiring moment rather than a convergence.

It also sets the split: **the workflow is seeded, the build script is not.** `build-site.mjs` stays in the pack and is read out of the mount by the seeded shim, exactly as the scheduler stub reads the engine's tick — so assembly logic keeps converging while only the file that *must* be frozen is frozen. The stub carries no settings either; those live on the declaration, so the frozen file has nothing that can go stale.

**Imports needed no rewrite.** `packs/<id>/` sits beside `engine/` in the canon and `.claudinite/shared/packs/<id>/` beside `.claudinite/shared/engine/` in a member, so `../../engine/…` resolves in both — and the staged site mirrors that shape for the same reason (flattening sends those imports above the site root and the page won't boot).

**No prose, no checks.** A page is not a practice; prose would bill every session in every declaring repo for something no session acts on.

## What's in the page

Two views, routed by URL — a **fleet overview** (members worst-first, with mount drift and never-ran detection that no single repo's page can show) and the **per-repo deep dive**. Client caching is SHA-keyed for content, ETag-revalidated for live data, 24h TTL for settled history: **21 requests → 4 cold-to-warm, zero rate limit spent on the warm load.** Access control is the viewer's own credential, always.

## Verification

- **103 tests** for the pack; **2001** in the full suite, all green. `check_the_world`: **0 blocking**.
- `build-site.mjs` exercised against a **simulated member mount** (engine + pack under `.claudinite/shared/`) in both modes: bare declaration → this repo's dashboard; `rosterFile` → fleet overview with only the names published, not the artifact's statistics.
- A test walks **every relative import in the staged site** and asserts it resolves inside the tree — the check that would have caught the earlier flattening bug without a browser.
- The packaged site served and driven in a browser: fleet → member → back, all imports resolving, using the config and roster the build actually generated.
- Adopted-but-not-yet-converged exits clean with no `_site`, so the deploy skips rather than replacing a working site with an empty artifact.

## Two things I checked rather than assumed

- **Declaring the pack in Sheepdog now would turn it red.** I tried it and ran Sheepdog's own checks: `declares unknown pack "claudinite-dashboard"` is a **blocking config error** until its mount carries the pack. So Sheepdog#232 is closed rather than re-pointed, and adoption there happens after this lands, via `adopt-pack`.
- The pack's `ruleRoutingGuidance` initially failed schema validation at 25 words against a 20-word cap — caught by the suite, trimmed.

**Not verified:** direct `api.github.com` is blocked by this session's proxy, so nothing has run against live GitHub — only real-data and simulated fixtures.

# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.

These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. The configure-pages action is a GitHub Action to enable Pages and extract various metadata about a site, and can also be used to configure various static site generators.

**Enablement Input and Permissions:**
The action tries to enable Pages for the repository if it is not already enabled. However, this option requires a token other than `GITHUB_TOKEN` to be provided, and in the context of a Personal Access Token, the `repo` scope or Pages write permission is required, while in the context of a GitHub App, the `administration:write` and `pages:write` permissions are required.

The deploy job must have a minimum of pages: write and id-token: write permissions. 2	// `pack.mjs` may and must carry. Everything a pack declares about itself is
3	// described here once, and `validateManifest` is the only thing that judges a
4	// manifest against it. The loader calls it on every pack it imports (canon and a
5	// consumer's own `local_packs/` alike), so a malformed or incomplete manifest
6	// surfaces as a blocking `config` error at load — the same class as invalid JSON
7	// in `.claudinite-checks.json`.
8	//
9	// WHY A SPEC AND NOT A CHECK. A required manifest field is part of the pack
10	// contract, not a conformance opinion about a repo's content: a conformance rule
11	// would have to be declared BY a pack, run only when that pack is active, and
12	// re-derive the manifest by reading its source text — enforcing the shape of the
13	// system from inside one of its members. The spec is upstream of every pack, so
14	// there is nothing to declare and nothing to parse.
15	//
16	// Dependency-free by the engine's module rule: no imports, no filesystem. The
17	// caller supplies the facts from disk (the `skills/` directory listing), so this
18	// module is pure and testable standalone.

20	// The routing budget. Both sides of `ruleRoutingGuidance` become one row of the
21	// pack catalog (packs/directory.GENERATED.md), which a session reads when deciding
22	// which pack owns a piece of content — so the cap keeps a row scannable: enough for

27	// `worldRules` audit repo state, `workRules` judge the change and session in
28	// front of you — so the two runners' partition is declared where a reader of the
29	// pack can see it, and a rule module never restates (or contradicts) it.

**No, it didn't — you found a real gap.** I checked rather than assumed: `updates/install.mjs` had no issue creation at all, no pack files issues at adoption, and `required_secrets` (the nearest precedent) only stamps a name into a workflow. Adoption seeded files and said nothing. [#942](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/942) I filed by hand, in the canon, covering the fleet-wide OAuth setup — but "enable Pages" is **per-adopting-repo**, and nothing would have filed it for the next member.

I first tried to delete the step rather than track it: `actions/configure-pages` has an `enablement` input, but it [requires a token other than `GITHUB_TOKEN`](https://github.com/actions/configure-pages) — a PAT with `repo`, or an app with `administration:write`. Holding a credential that wide in every member to save one click is a worse trade than naming the click, so it's genuinely irreducible.

So packs can now declare `adoptionHandover` — `{ step, breaks, done }`, which is the shape your own basics rule already demands for handing over human-only work. [`install.mjs`](updates/install.mjs) prints it at adoption, and [`adopt-pack`](packs/core/skills/adopt-pack/SKILL.md) files it as one tracking issue per adopting repo:

```
install: 1 step(s) only a human can do — open a tracking issue for these:
  [ ] (claudinite-dashboard) Enable GitHub Pages on this repo with source "GitHub Actions".
        while off: the deploy job fails on every run; the build still succeeds
        done when: the Pages URL serves the dashboard, and the workflow is green
```

The schema requires all three parts: `step` alone is a note someone has to interpret, `breaks` is how an adopter judges urgency, `done` is what lets the issue ever close.

Two things worth noting from doing it: the manifest vocabulary is **closed**, so my first attempt was a blocking config error — and the check's own fix text named the route (add it to [`pack-schema.mjs`](engine/pack_loader/pack-schema.mjs)). And a test failure turned out to be the install runner correctly exiting non-zero because a bare temp dir fails its self-test — the test was wrong, not the code.
